item.title: Knee — Deep Transverse Friction
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Knee and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or sitting with the knee supported in the position required by the technique.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the knee with hands close to the joint line and the limb fully supported.
stabilization: Stabilize femur, tibia or patella depending on the target.
contact: Use broad contact and avoid sustained compression over the fibular head/common peroneal nerve.
Identify a specific symptomatic tendon, ligament or muscle structure rather than rubbing a broad area.
Move transversely across the target tissue while minimizing sliding over the skin.
forceDirection: Use localized transverse loading that remains tolerable and does not provoke escalating pain.
dosage: Use short, symptom-guided bouts; progressive loading remains the main rehabilitation strategy for most tendinopathies.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Knee: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid routine manual therapy with suspected DVT, fracture, acute instability, infection or uncleared postoperative restriction.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Knee assessment → correct regional setup → Deep Transverse Friction → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Patellar Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Use only as a short-term adjunct for a localized, chronic patellar-tendon presentation; it is not the main treatment for patellar tendinopathy.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or long sitting with the knee supported in slight flexion so the quadriceps can relax and the tendon is easy to palpate.
subTechniques.contact: Identify the familiar symptomatic portion of the tendon—often near the inferior patellar pole. Use a fingertip or reinforced-finger contact across the tendon while stabilizing the overlying skin.
subTechniques.direction: Move strictly side-to-side across the tendon fibers with a small excursion. Do not rub longitudinally up and down the tendon.
subTechniques.dosage: Use a short, tolerable trial rather than prolonged painful friction. Reassess, then prioritize progressive tendon loading such as isometric/slow resistance according to irritability.
subTechniques.reassess: Pain during decline squat or other tendon-loading task, local tendon tenderness and loading tolerance.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The treatment target is a clinically identified tendon, not simply 'pain below the kneecap.' Loading progression matters far more than aggressive friction.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute tendon tear, marked swelling/heat, recent surgery or a highly irritable reactive presentation.

subTechniques.name: Quadriceps Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Selected adjunct for localized chronic quadriceps-tendon symptoms above the patella.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the knee supported in slight flexion and quadriceps relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Use precise transverse contact over the symptomatic tendon just superior to the patella while avoiding direct patellar pressure.
subTechniques.direction: Small side-to-side movement across the tendon fibers.
subTechniques.dosage: Short tolerable bouts followed by graded quadriceps loading.
subTechniques.reassess: Pain with squat/step, resisted knee extension and local tendon tenderness.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Differentiate quadriceps tendon pain from patellofemoral pain before treating the tendon.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute tear or reactive inflammatory flare.
